title: Investment and Financial Markets
summary: Learn how investing works: risk and return, compounding, shares and bonds, diversification and asset allocation, funds and the true cost of fees, investor behaviour and how to spot scams.
audience: Young professionals, students and anyone starting to invest

body.p: Saving keeps money safe and available, for example in a bank account, for short-term needs and emergencies. Investing puts money into assets that are expected to grow over the long term, accepting that their value will rise and fall along the way. Inflation makes this important: money left idle loses purchasing power each year.

Higher expected returns usually come with higher risk, meaning bigger swings in value and a greater chance of loss over short periods. Cash is low risk and low return; bonds are in between; shares (equities) and property have higher long-term returns with more volatility. Anyone promising high returns with no risk is almost certainly running a scam.

list: Pay off expensive debt, such as credit cards, first; its interest usually exceeds investment returns.
Build an emergency fund of several months' expenses.
Define goals and time horizons: money needed within about three years should not be in volatile assets.
Understand your tolerance for seeing your investments fall.

body.tip: This course is education, not personal financial advice. For decisions about your own money, consider a licensed, independent financial adviser.

body.p: Compound growth means earning returns on previous returns. Over long periods it produces dramatic results.

list: A lump sum of R10 000 growing at 8% a year becomes 10 000 x 1.08¹⁰, about R21 589, after 10 years.
The rule of 72 estimates doubling time: at 8%, money doubles in about 72 / 8 = 9 years.
Investing R1000 a month for 20 years at 10% a year (compounded monthly) grows to about R759 369, although only R240 000 was paid in.
Starting early matters more than investing large amounts later, because the money has longer to compound.

body.p: What matters is growth after inflation. If investments return 9% while inflation is 6%, the real return is roughly 3% a year. A savings account paying 4% when inflation is 6% loses purchasing power.

body.tip: Automate a monthly investment on payday; consistency beats trying to pick the perfect moment.

lessons.title: Shares, bonds and how markets work

body.p: Shares are small ownership stakes in companies, bought and sold on stock exchanges such as the Johannesburg Stock Exchange, the Nigerian Exchange, the Nairobi Securities Exchange and the Ghana Stock Exchange. Shareholders gain from rising share prices and dividends, but prices can fall sharply.

list: Price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio = share price / earnings per share. A R50 share with earnings of R5 per share has a P/E of 10.
Dividend yield = dividend per share / price. A R2 dividend on a R50 share is a 4% yield.
Market capitalisation = share price x number of shares.

body.p: A bond is a loan to a government or company that pays regular interest (coupons) and returns the face value at maturity. A bond with a face value of R1000 and a 10% coupon pays R100 a year. If interest rates rise, existing bond prices fall: if this bond trades at R950, its current yield is 100 / 950, about 10.5%. Government bonds of stable countries are lower risk than company bonds; higher yields compensate for higher default risk.

body.tip: A falling share price is not a bargain by itself; check whether the company's business has changed.

body.p: Diversification spreads money across many investments so that one failure does not ruin the portfolio. Owning 30 companies across different industries and countries is far less risky than owning one, while expected returns stay similar.

Asset allocation, the split between shares, bonds, property and cash, drives most of a portfolio's long-term behaviour. A portfolio of 60% shares expected to return 12% and 40% bonds expected to return 7% has an expected return of 0.6 x 12 + 0.4 x 7 = 10% a year, with less volatility than shares alone.

list: Longer time horizons can usually hold more shares.
Rebalance periodically back to target weights, which means selling some of what has risen and buying what has fallen.
Diversify across countries and currencies as well as companies.
Do not hold too much of your employer's shares; your job and savings would depend on one company.

body.tip: Write down your target allocation and the rules for rebalancing, so emotions do not drive decisions in market panics.

lessons.title: Funds, ETFs and the cost of fees

body.p: Most people invest through pooled funds that hold many assets and are run by professional managers.

list: Unit trusts or mutual funds: actively managed funds that try to beat the market, usually with higher fees.
Index funds and exchange-traded funds (ETFs): track a market index at low cost and trade on stock exchanges.
Retirement funds and pension schemes often offer tax advantages, with rules on access.

body.p: Suppose R100 000 grows for 20 years at 9% a year before fees. With fees of 0.5% a year, the net return is 8.5% and the investment grows to about R511 205. With fees of 2%, the net return is 7% and it grows to about R386 968. The higher fee costs about R124 236, more than the original investment.
Check the total expense ratio and any platform, advice and performance fees. Most actively managed funds do not consistently beat low-cost index funds after fees over long periods.

body.tip: Compare funds by total costs, strategy and long-term net returns, not by last year's top performance.

body.p: Behaviour often decides results more than investment knowledge. Common mistakes include panic-selling after falls, buying popular investments after big rises, checking prices obsessively and trading too often, which adds costs and taxes.

list: Guaranteed high returns with little or no risk.
Pressure to invest quickly or recruit friends and family (pyramid and Ponzi schemes pay early investors with money from new ones).
Unregistered schemes: check that the firm is licensed with the financial regulator, such as the FSCA in South Africa, the SEC in Nigeria, the CMA in Kenya or the SEC in Ghana.
Complex or secret strategies nobody can explain.
Requests to pay into personal accounts or with cryptocurrency only.

body.p: Crypto-assets can rise and fall very quickly, are often lightly regulated and are frequently used in scams; treat them as high-risk speculation, and only with money you can afford to lose.

body.tip: If you cannot explain how an investment makes money in two sentences, do not invest in it.
